title: insert clickbaity title here
author: Caiti Wade
summary: Caiti Wade takes aim at a Herald Sun headline claiming almost nine in ten teachers do not know how to teach, a distortion of a Centre for Independent Studies report by Trisha Jha. She explains the report's actual purpose, which was to find where teacher knowledge gaps block the use of the science of learning and to target initial teacher education and professional learning accordingly. Drawing on her own experience, she describes an education degree that never mentioned cognitive science and a lecturer who barred explicit instruction from an assignment. She argues that some critics reject CIS research because of the organisation rather than the evidence, citing the pile-on after a classroom behaviour report. Her conclusion is that identifying a system-level gap is not blaming teachers, and that the profession has been let down by its preparation.
points: Wade separates a misleading headline from the research beneath it, noting that the report itself is supportive of teachers.
Her own teacher-training story shows a gap in science-of-learning content and active discouragement of explicit instruction.
She contends that disliking a think tank is not a reason to dismiss its data, pointing to recurring pile-ons against CIS reports.
The knowledge-gap findings are aimed at system-level reform of initial teacher education and professional learning, not at individual teachers.
She warns that sensational framing derails discussion into whether research insults teachers instead of how to support them.
quotes: The article itself, however, isn’t the headline. Although, judging by the uproar online this week, I’m not convinced many have made it past the headline and into the article.

Comments from teachers in this study revealed a frustration at what is essentially a knowledge gap when it comes to implementing the science of learning in classrooms, potentially stemming from initial teacher education degrees.
Instead, I came across cognitive load theory entirely myself through a paper by John Hattie that sent me down a rabbit hole of personal research.
My teaching was largely inefficient. I would teach, then wander the classroom and find that half of my class had the same misconception, so I’d be back at the whiteboard addressing this.
News flash: you don’t have to like CIS as an organisation to appreciate their research, or elements of it.
It would be of spectacular irony if the research intended to address these gaps became another casualty of sensationalist headlines, misrepresentation and the general discourse that follows.

That’s a real shame, because this research wasn’t conducted to tell teachers they’re not good enough. It was conducted to better understand how we can ensure they’re given the knowledge and support they deserve.
